turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, before the doctor steps in, your blood pressure is 148 over 86, heart rate is 76, and your oxygen is 97 percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): 148 over 86, yeah, the cuff at the drugstore said about the same last Tuesday. Parking was a mess, somebody boxed me in by the cart return.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Okonkwo. Thanks for those, Maria. You booked this as a check-up. Anything particular, or are we just looking you over?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Just a check-up. My daughter has been after me for months. I'm 63, I still mow my own lawn, I don't know what she's so wound up about.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any chest pain, or do you get short of breath?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Chest pain? No. I don't have chest pain. I get a little winded if I rush, but who doesn't.
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He hesitates on the stairs at the house. I'm there weekday mornings, and I've watched him stop halfway up more than once.

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, fine. It's not pain. When I climb the stairs, or if I'm walking fast, I get this tight feeling across my chest, like a band, and if I stop it eases off in about a minute.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): So rest settles it in about a minute, and it's the stairs or a fast walk that brings it on. Does it show up when you're just sitting?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not when I'm sitting. Only if I push it. The squirrels have taken over the new bird feeder, though, and I am losing that war.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Squirrels can stay out of the note. How long has that tight feeling been going on? Can you date it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I don't know. Maybe a couple months, maybe longer. I can't really put a start on it. It kind of snuck up.
[SEG0013] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He downplays stuff. Getting him through the door today was a project. He tried to bargain for donuts in the parking lot.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): When the tightness comes, do you sweat, feel sick to your stomach, or get pain down your arm?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating. It doesn't go down my arm. Stomach's fine too, I think. I just stop, it eases, I get on with it.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on? Walk me through them.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Lisinopril, ten milligrams, one every morning for my blood pressure. I've been on that for years. And a baby aspirin, 81 milligrams, but I take that on and off. Some weeks I forget.

[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I set the lisinopril out with breakfast and he does swallow that one. The aspirin bottle barely moves. My husband takes metformin for his diabetes, 500 milligrams twice a day, but that's my husband, not Mr. Hale.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, don't write his metformin down for me. My neighbor is all about fish oil too. I never started that. She says her joints feel brand new, good for her.

[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Metformin and the fish oil are not yours, so they're out. Thinking out loud: tightness across the chest when you climb or walk fast, gone after about a minute of rest, you're 63, pressure today is 148 over 86, and you're on lisinopril. That pattern can be angina, the heart asking for more blood than the pipes deliver when you exert. I wouldn't call it definite sitting here.

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina, wonderful. My uncle had a heart attack at 70, the whole family panicked, he lived in Ohio. I feel fine in this chair, though. The chair is awful, somebody should hear about that.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll put your uncle's heart attack in the family history. Chairs are not my department. Today I want an ECG, and bloods, a lipid panel and a basic metabolic panel.
[SEG0023] person_1 (NURSE): I can run the ECG in the next room once you're done, and the lab's open if he goes straight over for the draw.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Am I supposed to be fasting? I had coffee and a blueberry muffin already. The muffin was dry as cardboard. That place on 4th is really slipping.

[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): With a muffin on board, today's lipid panel won't be a true fasting result. We'll still draw it. I can repeat a fasting lipid later if the numbers are hard to interpret. Not an automatic second needle.
[SEG0026] person_4 (CAREGIVER): What about the aspirin, should he stop it or keep going?
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep it, but take the 81 milligrams every single day, not only the weeks you remember. And don't skip the lisinopril in the mornings.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Every day, got it. Can I still finish the fence this weekend? Three sections left, and they're saying the weather holds.

[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Light yard work is fine. If that tight feeling starts, stop and rest. If it lasts more than a few minutes, or you sweat, get sick to your stomach, or it moves into your jaw or arm, call 911. Don't drive yourself.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): 911, sure, I'm not gonna be a hero about it. My sister keeps texting me biotin articles, though. She takes ten thousand micrograms for her hair. Her hair is her entire personality. I've still got mine.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Your sister's biotin isn't your medicine, so I'm leaving it off. Let me have a listen.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Heartbeat is regular, no murmur. Lungs are clear. There's no swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you, skinny ankles, always. So am I being dramatic, or is this a real thing?

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not being dramatic. My working impression is possible stable angina, but the ECG and the labs have to speak before I'd go further. We'll book you back in one week to go over the results.
[SEG0035] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him to that visit, and I'll park the aspirin right next to the lisinopril so it actually gets taken.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): One week, alright. If the squirrels demolish the feeder before then, I don't want to hear about it.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

omissions.text: Denied chest pain when specifically asked ('Chest pain? No. I don't have chest pain.').
Exertional chest tightness is specifically described as 'not pain.'
Caregiver reported he hesitates on the stairs and has stopped halfway up more than once.
Family history detail is recorded incompletely: the uncle's heart attack occurred at age 70.
